unmergedDoubts.whyNotMerged: IH's single mechanism spans registry, prepare/dispatch/finalize pipeline AND parallel dispatch in one package, while dsh splits the same ground into three mechanisms. It was placed in the registry row (its 'registry is the single enforcement point' half), so the pipeline row and the parallel row show no ih member although IH implements aspects of both. A reader should not read those two rows as 'IH has nothing here'.

Both drive the same `diff`-package structuredPatch with a DIFF_TIMEOUT_MS bound and hunk-context constant, but cc-custom's mechanism is the Edit/Write tool as a whole (mtime staleness critical section, curly-quote fallback, quote-style preservation), so it belongs with the file-editing family; only the diff sub-part overlaps IH's standalone diff engine.

MERGED into one row, not left apart: dsh deliberately ships str_replace_editor as an ALTERNATIVE editor beside tool-fs, so the same source contributes two mechanisms to the file-editing row. Flagged here because a reader scanning member counts may otherwise read the double dsh entry as an error.

Both are tool-side sandbox policy, but dsh's is a path fence plus escalation-field advertisement on the fs/shell tools, while codex's is a two-attempt approval/retry ladder around every tool runtime. Merging would have claimed a fence and an escalation ladder are one capability.

dsh's retention library is the bounding primitive and spill-policy is the tool-facing policy; other sources bundle both in one mechanism. Kept apart because dsh's retainer is imported by the terminal renderer, search core and jobs tool, i.e. it is broader than tool-result spill, so folding it in would have hidden that.

Both cc-custom mechanisms are present-but-inert (a feature gate that is always false). They are the same capability family as the tool-batch executors, but merging them would have hidden the unwired status, so each is its own row with an inert-reflecting disposition.

All three intervene on a degenerate tool-call loop, but cc-custom's keys on a specific command pattern (leading `sleep`) and is compiled out, while dsh's and opencode's key on identical repeated calls. Trigger and mechanism differ enough that a merge would have overstated agreement.

grok's doom-loop recovery is server-signalled (a non-standard SSE event) and is bundled with a generic backoff ladder, whereas opencode's is client-detected and raises a permission ask. Kept with the retry mechanism because that is grok's own framing.

codex's unified_exec is simultaneously codex's default SHELL tool and a persistent PTY session manager. Placed with PTY sessions because that is its distinctive design, which leaves the shell-execution row without a codex member even though codex does execute shell commands.

codex's mechanism is a bundle (sandbox-aware filesystem abstraction + nucleo fuzzy file search + the shared output-truncation policy). It was placed in the search row for its search half; the fs-abstraction and truncation-policy halves could not be separated without inventing member names.

dsh has both a generic per-tool cooperative timeout wrapper and per-process clamping/deadline classification inside the shell executors. The generic wrapper is not the same mechanism as a process timeout, so the two stayed in different rows.

fork's host shims do sit at registry assembly (adapting legacy host definitions onto the core registry), so they were considered for the registry row, but they are migration glue rather than a capability, and merging would have implied the fork's registry and its legacy adapter are one design.
